title: Seaming two live edges in crochet
subtitle: How to join two active rows of crochet without fastening off either piece first
excerpt: When both pieces still have an active loop, you can join them directly with a slip stitch or double crochet seam rather than fastening off and sewing. It gives a clean, stretchy join.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book.

glossaryTerms.definition: The active loop remaining on the hook at the end of an unfinished piece, as distinct from a fastened-off tail.
The shortest crochet stitch, made by drawing the working yarn through both the stitch and the loop on the hook in one motion, adding almost no height.

content.text: When two crocheted pieces both have a

on the hook, you can join them directly without fastening off either piece first. This is the crochet version of the knitting three-needle cast-off. Hold both active edges together and work through both at once. It suits shoulder seams and any join where fastening off and sewing each piece first would take extra time.

Both pieces should have the same stitch count along the joining edge. Hold them with the edges aligned, wrong sides together for a visible seam or right sides together for a hidden seam. Place the live loop from the first piece onto the hook. The second piece has its live loop set aside temporarily (or is held close at the edge to align stitches).
Slip stitch join on live edges
Hold the two pieces edge to edge with the hook through the live loop of the working piece.
Insert the hook into the first stitch of the second piece (the live loop or the top of the final stitch).
through both layers: yarn over, draw through both edge stitches and through the loop on the hook in one motion.
Move to the next stitch of each piece in turn and repeat across.
Fasten off and weave in when the seam is complete.
Double crochet join for a stronger seam

For a firmer seam with a visible ridge, substitute double crochet for the slip stitch in step 3. The join becomes a decorative structural element rather than an invisible seam. Use a matching or contrasting colour depending on whether the seam should show.

items.symptom: The pieces shift and the stitch alignment is off mid-seam
items.cause: The two pieces are not pinned or held flush before starting.
items.fix: Place stitch markers through corresponding stitches on both pieces at the midpoint and each quarter before starting. Work toward each marker in turn.

items.symptom: The seam is much tighter than the body
items.cause: Slip stitch seams can pull tight, especially worked in a single colour.
items.fix: Go up one hook size for the seam, or switch to double crochet which adds a little height and reduces the pulling.

content.text: For garments where shoulder seams matter to fit, practise on two identical tension swatches first. The seam should flex with the fabric and not restrict movement when the garment is worn.
